guidance.title: Designing across an exon–exon junction
guidance.summary: This endpoint scores primers against the template it was given; it does not know where the exons are. Genomic DNA is the usual contaminant in an RNA prep, and placing the pair so that gDNA cannot be amplified is a decision about the transcript, taken before the sequence is pasted in.

sections.heading: Where to put the pair
rules: Put one primer across an exon–exon junction, so the primer has no contiguous match in genomic DNA — the intron sits where the junction is.
Leave at least 7 bases of that primer on the shorter exon. With three or four, the longer half still anneals well enough to amplify genomic DNA and the design buys nothing.
Do not leave only one or two bases past the junction at the 3' end. A single terminal mismatch is extended often enough that it is not reliable discrimination.

If no junction suits, fall back to flanking: put the two primers in different exons with an intron of 1 kb or more between them. The cDNA product is short, the genomic one is too long to amplify under qPCR cycling, or is obvious by size.

sections.heading: When a junction cannot save you
rules: Single-exon genes have no junction at all. Treat the RNA with DNase I and rely on the −RT control.

Processed pseudogenes are reverse-transcribed mRNA inserted back into the genome: they contain the junction, so a junction-spanning primer amplifies them perfectly well. That is the case the off-target screen on this page is for — paste the pseudogene or the paralogs into the screening box.
Highly similar paralogs and recent gene families do the same thing. Screen against them explicitly rather than assuming the junction covers it.

sections.heading: The rest of the design
rules: Keep the product between 70 and 150 bp. Past about 250 bp the amplification efficiency drifts away from the doubling a Cq assumes, and the quantification stops being linear.
Aim for a Tm of 58–62 °C with the two primers within 2 °C of each other, and 40–60% GC.
Avoid four or more identical bases in a row, G runs most of all.
Keep no more than two G or C in the last five bases: a sticky 3' end mis-primes.
Check for common SNPs under the primer, especially within five bases of the 3' end — a variant there costs an allele.

sections.heading: On every plate
rules: Run a −RT control. No primer design removes the need for it; it is the measurement that tells you whether any of the above worked.
Confirm a single melt peak, or a single band, before trusting a Cq.

notes: 40 positions were tried across the template, not every one — these are the best of those, not the best possible.

Nothing was screened against. For qRT-PCR the template is a genome or a transcriptome, where mis-priming is the usual reason a reaction fails — these pairs are thermodynamically sound and unproven for specificity. Pass the locus with its flanks, the paralogs, or the transcript panel.
Exon structure is not considered here — this endpoint does not take exon boundaries. See `guidance` for how to place the pair so that contaminating genomic DNA is not amplified alongside the cDNA.
